newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf seen needing major infrastructure investment.
newsitem.headline: Gulf seen needing major infrastructure investment.

text.p: Billions of dollars need to be injected annually to upgrade the Gulf's infrastructure to meet strong demand in a region that has one of the world's highest population growth rates, industry experts said on Monday.

Speaking on the sidelines of the Middle East Infrastructure Development Congress in Dubai, they said the days when oil-rich governments were willing or could afford to pay for huge capital projects like water desalination and power plants were over.
"The capital requirement is so huge that we need private sector investment," said Saleh al-Omair, who served as vice minister of finance in Saudi Arabia until last year.
Enron Development Corp president Joseph Sutton said in some countries, like Saudi Arabia, demand within the next 10 years would be double the current installed capacity.

The World Energy Council has said electricity demand in the past two decades has been growing faster in the Arab world -- particularly the Gulf's Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman and United Arab Emirates -- than any other area.

Chief economist at Saudi Arabia's National Commercial Bank, Henry Azzam, estimated that $10 billion a year would have to be spent on upgrading basic infrastructure in the six Gulf Arab states over the next 10 years. "This is not insurmountable," he said, adding the domestic market had the means to finance it.
Analysts said slashed capital spending by states after years of deficit budgets amid low oil prices meant more private sector involvement in funding and providing infrastructure was likely.
"The capital requirement is so huge and with budget tightening it can't really be done by governments," Omair said.
Parsons Brinckerhoff Infrastructure Development Co director Stephen Weinstein said Gulf governments needed to look at changing laws to allow international parties to be involved.
"Gulf states have a lot going for them -- strong and stable governments, accomplished and creative banks, a willingness to embrace the world of private finance and expanding economies.
"What is needed is a clear system for involving private capital, making it a predictable rather than ad-hoc process."
Apart from the financing issue, Gulf states needed to review heavily subsidised power and water tariffs to discourage wastage and enforce demand management.
"We are using water like we live next to the Mississippi," said Fareed Zedan, chairman of a group carrying out an official study into restructuring the Saudi power sector.

"We need to move prices to a certain level where we stop this waste. If someone is basing his calculations (for setting up an industrial concern) on cheap electricity, he should not be there. These are dinosaurs, white elephants," Omair said.
Zedan suggested a staggered tariff system be introduced, in which different rates are charged for low income and more affluent households and industrial consumers.
